newsitem.title: CHINA: Pro-China politician to lead post-handover HK legislature.
newsitem.headline: Pro-China politician to lead post-handover HK legislature.

text.p: A former colonial official who switched allegiance to China was chosen on Saturday to head the controversial body that will repeal laws protecting civil rights in Hong Kong after it reverts to China this year.
Governor Chris Patten immediately denounced the occasion as a "bad day for Hong Kong" and said the provisional legislature had no "legitimacy, no credibility and no authority".

Rita Fan, 54, a former Hong Kong legislator and cabinet member and a key player in committees overseeing the handover, received 33 votes to 27 for her only rival, Andrew Wong, president of the incumbent elected Legislative Council (Legco).
The meeting took place amid a rift between China and the outgoing colonial power, Britain, over Bejing's plans to roll back civil liberties in Hong Kong after the handover on July 1.
The 60-member provisional legislature met across the border in Shenzhen to avoid legal challenges to its legitimacy in Hong Kong, where opponents have branded it as illegal.
It was the first meeting of the body, which was picked by a Chinese-appointed panel in December to replace the elected Legco and undo the democratic reforms of Governor Chris Patten.
Fan is an ex-Legco member who sat on the Executive Council advising the British governor before Patten arrived in 1992.

The vote was by secret ballot at the Shenzhen State Guesthouse, a two-storey luxury mansion with glittering crystal chandeliers and a grand staircase that normally hosts bigwigs of the ruling Chinese Communist Party.
Fan will occupy a key role as arbiter of legislative debates, much like the speaker in a parliament.

But her job in the future Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) will be highly controversial as she will be heading a legislature whose legal credentials may be challenged by Hong Kong's pro-democracy groups and by Britain.

Britain, which hands the colony back to China at midnight on June 30, has challenged Beijing to let the World Court in The Hague rule on whether the provisional legislature violates the treaty governing the transfer of sovereignty.
Fan made clear after her victory that the new body would not necessarily adopt all the procedures as the elected Legco.

"I believe it may not be totally appropriate for us to think that everything, the manner, every small minute detail in which the current Legislative Council in Hong Kong operates, will be followed by the provisional legislature," she told reporters.

A fresh quarrel flared this week when Britain attacked China over a plan to roll back Hong Kong's Bill of Rights and laws on freedom of association. The Amnesty International human rights group said China would use the changes to restrict freedom.
China called the protests unwise. Its top official on Hong Kong, Lu Ping, said the changes were necessary.

"There are laws which the SAR government needs to amend or repeal -- the Public Order Ordinance, for instance, which gives freedom only to a small group of people, while it affects the rights of the majority," Lu, who is head of China's Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, told reporters.

Hong Kong's post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa said the body would examine the definition of "permanent resident", the flag of the new Hong Kong, its 1997/1998 budget, and the appointment of judges for the Court of Final Appeal and the High Court.
